## How to Save Money on Utilities

If your utility bills feel unpredictable, you are not imagining it. Electricity, heating, water, internet, and phone costs can take a large bite out of a monthly budget, especially when several small charges rise at once. The good news is that learning **how to save money on utilities** does not have to mean living in the dark or taking cold showers.

The strongest approach is to find the few charges you can control, make changes that match your home and habits, and track the savings. Start with the quick fixes below, then use the larger upgrades when the payback makes sense.

## Start with a one-month utility audit

Before changing anything, pull out the last 12 months of bills if you have them. List the amount due, usage, rate plan, fees, and billing period for each service. A bill that is higher this month may reflect more usage, a rate increase, or simply a longer billing cycle.

Create five categories in your spending tracker: electricity, heating fuel or gas, water and sewer, internet, and mobile service. This gives you a baseline and makes it easier to spot a recurring jump. Pennywise can help you see these bills alongside rent, groceries, and subscriptions, rather than treating them as isolated surprises.

Look for these signals:

- Electricity use that rises even when your routine has not changed
- A water bill that is consistently higher than similar months
- Promotional internet or phone pricing that has expired
- Fees for equipment, paper statements, late payments, or add-ons
- A rate plan that does not fit when your household uses the most energy

## 1. Set your thermostat for savings, not discomfort

Heating and cooling are often the biggest controllable parts of a home energy bill. The U.S. Department of Energy says you can save up to 10% a year on heating and cooling by turning your thermostat back 7 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit for eight hours a day from its normal setting. The exact result depends on your climate, insulation, and system, but the principle is reliable: avoid heating or cooling an empty home at the same level as an occupied one.

Use a programmable or smart thermostat if it fits your system. Schedule a more moderate setting when everyone is asleep or away, then return to a comfortable temperature shortly before people get home. Renters can often use a basic programmable model, but check the lease and compatibility first.

## 2. Seal drafts before buying expensive equipment

A small gap around a window, exterior door, or pipe can make your heating and cooling system work harder all season. Weatherstripping, door sweeps, caulk, and outlet gaskets are low-cost fixes that can noticeably improve comfort.

On a cool or windy day, feel around window frames, doors, attic hatches, and where cables or pipes enter the home. Seal gaps that do not need ventilation. Do not block appliance vents, fireplace vents, or any combustion-air opening. If you rent, ask your landlord before making permanent changes.

## 3. Use ceiling fans in the right direction

Ceiling fans do not lower room temperature, but they help people feel cooler by moving air across skin. In summer, run the fan counterclockwise while you are in the room. In winter, a low clockwise setting can gently circulate warm air that collects near the ceiling.

Turn fans off when rooms are empty. A fan cools people, not furniture.

## 4. Cut standby power from the easy targets

Many devices draw small amounts of electricity while they are idle. You do not need to unplug every clock in the house, but it is worth targeting clusters of equipment that are rarely used.

Plug a television, game console, streaming box, and speakers into a power strip, then switch it off when the setup is not in use. Do the same for a home office, provided you do not interrupt a device that needs to stay on. Chargers should come out of the wall after the device is charged.

## 5. Change laundry habits before replacing appliances

Laundry can be an easy place to lower utility bills. Wash full loads when possible, use cold water for everyday clothes, and choose the shortest cycle that gets the job done. Cold-water detergent is designed to work at lower temperatures, and heating water is often the most energy-intensive part of washing.

Clean the dryer lint filter every load. Dry similar fabrics together, avoid over-drying, and use a drying rack for items that do not need a machine. If you are buying a new unit, compare the estimated annual energy use on the EnergyGuide label, not just the purchase price.

## 6. Make the water heater work less

Hot water quietly affects both water and energy spending. Shorter showers help, but so do practical maintenance steps. Repair dripping faucets, insulate accessible hot-water pipes, and make sure the water heater temperature is not set higher than necessary.

The Department of Energy generally recommends 120 degrees Fahrenheit for most households. That setting can reduce energy use and lower scalding risk. Households with specific health needs should ask a qualified professional before changing the setting.

A low-flow showerhead is another useful upgrade. It can reduce hot-water use while still providing a comfortable shower, particularly when paired with an efficient fixture rather than a restrictive bargain model.

## 7. Find water leaks quickly

A running toilet can waste a surprising amount of water. To test one, put a few drops of food coloring in the tank and wait 10 to 15 minutes without flushing. Color appearing in the bowl usually means the flapper needs attention.

Also check under sinks, behind the washing machine, near the water heater, and around outdoor spigots. If your water meter changes while all water is off, you may have a hidden leak. Report suspected underground or building-system leaks promptly.

## 8. Cook with the smallest efficient tool

Use a microwave, toaster oven, pressure cooker, slow cooker, or air fryer for small meals when it makes sense. These appliances often use less energy than heating a full-size oven for a single serving. When you do use the oven, cook multiple items at once and avoid opening the door repeatedly.

Match pot size to burner size, keep lids on pots, and use an electric kettle for water when you need only a small amount. These are modest savings individually, but kitchen habits repeat every day.

## 9. Adjust your refrigerator and freezer

Keep refrigerator coils and vents clear, check that door seals close tightly, and leave room for air to circulate. A refrigerator works best when it is reasonably full but not packed so tightly that air cannot move.

Set the refrigerator between 35 and 38 degrees Fahrenheit and the freezer at 0 degrees Fahrenheit. Colder settings do not keep food safer once you are already in the recommended range. Let hot leftovers cool briefly before refrigerating, and cover liquids so the compressor does not have to manage extra moisture.

## 10. Choose the electricity rate plan that matches your schedule

Some utilities offer time-of-use pricing, which charges different rates at different times of day. It can be a good deal if you can move laundry, dishwashing, and electric-vehicle charging outside expensive peak periods. It can cost more if most of your use is locked into the peak window.

Check your utility website for rate options and read the peak hours carefully. Compare your actual hourly usage, if available, before switching. Do not choose a plan based on a single low advertised rate.

## 11. Ask about budget billing and assistance programs

Budget billing spreads expected annual utility costs into more even monthly payments. It does not reduce total energy use, but it can make cash flow easier to manage. Review the true-up terms so you understand whether you could owe a larger balance later.

If income changes or a high bill creates a hardship, contact the utility early. Many providers offer payment arrangements, efficiency kits, weatherization support, or referrals to local assistance. In the United States, LIHEAP may help eligible households with home energy bills and energy-related repairs.

## 12. Renegotiate internet before you cancel it

Internet bills often rise after an introductory deal ends. Check your current speed, monthly price, equipment rental, data limits, and add-ons. Many households pay for a speed tier they do not need.

Call or chat with the provider and ask whether there is a current plan with the same or better service at a lower price. Be polite, specific, and prepared to compare alternatives. If buying your own compatible modem or router eliminates a monthly rental fee, calculate the payback period first.

## 13. Treat phone service like any other subscription

Review every line on the account, insurance option, device payment, and streaming bundle. If your phone is paid off, compare prepaid and lower-cost carriers that use the same major networks. A switch can be worthwhile, but make sure coverage is strong where you live and work.

Keep your number by asking for the account number and transfer PIN before moving service. Do not cancel the old line until the number has transferred successfully.

## 14. Replace bulbs strategically

LED bulbs use much less energy and last longer than traditional incandescent bulbs. Replace the lights that are on for several hours a day first, such as kitchen, living room, exterior, and hallway fixtures. Check bulb brightness, color temperature, and dimmer compatibility so you buy a product you will actually use.

## 15. Maintain heating and cooling equipment

Replace or clean HVAC filters on the schedule recommended for your system. Keep outdoor equipment clear of leaves and debris, and do not close too many supply vents in an attempt to force air elsewhere. If rooms heat or cool unevenly, an annual service visit can uncover airflow, thermostat, or duct issues.

For a major repair or replacement, request more than one quote. The cheapest equipment is not always the lowest-cost choice over its life, but a high-efficiency upgrade should have a realistic payback based on your actual utility rates.

## 16. Avoid false savings

Some changes sound frugal but create bigger costs later. Turning off heat completely during freezing weather can lead to burst pipes. Skipping necessary maintenance can shorten appliance life. Choosing the cheapest electricity plan without checking fees can backfire.

Focus first on habits and upgrades that reduce waste without adding risk: stopping leaks, scheduling the thermostat, sealing drafts, using efficient fixtures, and removing services you do not use.

## 17. Put the savings somewhere useful

When a bill drops, move the difference intentionally. You could add it to an emergency fund, pay down high-interest debt, or save for a planned expense. Without a destination, small recurring savings often disappear into everyday spending.

Try this simple system:

1. Record your average utility cost for the last three months.
2. Pick two changes to try for the next billing cycle.
3. Compare usage and cost against a similar month, accounting for weather.
4. Transfer part of any savings to a goal the day you pay the bill.

For more ways to make your money go further, read our guides on [how to avoid overdraft fees](/blog/how-to-avoid-overdraft-fees), [how to build an emergency fund from scratch](/blog/how-to-build-emergency-fund-from-scratch), and the [no-spend challenge](/blog/no-spend-challenge-complete-guide).

## Frequently asked questions

### What uses the most electricity in a home?

In many homes, heating and cooling are major electricity users, followed by water heating, large appliances, lighting, and electronics. Your biggest source depends on climate, fuel type, home size, and appliance age. Your utility bill or an energy monitor can show where to investigate first.

### What is the fastest way to lower a utility bill?

The fastest wins are usually fixing leaks, changing thermostat schedules, reducing hot-water use, turning off unnecessary standby devices, and calling internet or phone providers to remove fees or switch plans.

### Does unplugging appliances really save money?

It can, especially for groups of electronics that stay in standby mode. Focus on entertainment centers, office setups, chargers, and equipment used only occasionally. A switchable power strip makes the habit easier.

### Is budget billing worth it?

Budget billing can make monthly costs more predictable, which is helpful for planning. It does not lower total annual use, and many programs reconcile the account periodically. Read the terms and still work on reducing consumption.
